33110: His mother Athaliah and the house of Ahab advise him to do wickedly, 'to his undoing'.
33112: He fights alongside his uncle Joram of Israel at Ramoth-gilead and then visits the wounded Joram at Jezreel.
33114: Caught up in Jehu's revolt, he flees, is wounded near Ibleam and dies at Megiddo. He is buried in Jerusalem for Jehoshaphat's sake.
33115: Ahaziah, son of Jehoram and Athaliah, reigned over Judah for one year (841 BC). The verdict of the text is that he did evil, following the house of Ahab, to which he was related by marriage. Visiting his wounded uncle at Jezreel, he was swept up in Jehu's revolt and killed. His death opened the way for his mother Athaliah to seize power and try to wipe out the royal family.
33116: Twenty-two when he began to reign, reigned one year; his mother was Athaliah (2 Kgs 8:26). Did evil like the house of Ahab (2 Kgs 8:27). Killed by Jehu's men (2 Kgs 9:27). 2 Chr 22:2 in the Hebrew says forty-two, which would make him older than his father; most versions follow 2 Kgs 8:26 and some Greek and Syriac witnesses with twenty-two (scholarly-consensus that forty-two is a copying error).
33117: Young, easily led and eager to belong to his powerful relatives in the north.
33122: While Jezebel is killing the LORD's prophets, he hides a hundred of them in two caves and feeds them bread and water.
33124: Sent by Ahab to search for grass, he meets Elijah, who tells him to announce him to Ahab. Afraid Elijah will vanish and Ahab will kill him, he hesitates, but Elijah swears to appear, and Obadiah carries the message.
33125: Obadiah was the official in charge of King Ahab's palace and a man who 'feared the LORD greatly'. Working inside Ahab's government, he secretly saved a hundred prophets from Jezebel's purge. During the drought he became the reluctant go-between who arranged the meeting of Elijah and Ahab that led to the contest on Mount Carmel. He is generally distinguished from the prophet Obadiah who wrote the book.
33126: Over Ahab's household; feared the LORD greatly (1 Kgs 18:3). Hid and fed a hundred prophets (1 Kgs 18:4). Feared the LORD from his youth (1 Kgs 18:12). Arranged the meeting of Elijah and Ahab (1 Kgs 18:16).
33128: The Talmud (Sanhedrin 39b) identifies him with the prophet Obadiah, an Edomite convert, and later Jewish lore names him as husband of the widow helped by Elisha in 2 Kings 4 (tradition).
33129: Often discussed as a model, or a test case, of serving faithfully inside a corrupt government. Most scholars date the book of Obadiah much later and do not identify him with its author (scholarly-consensus).
33130: Careful, devout and anxious; a loyal insider who weighs every risk and still does the right thing.
33137: A wealthy woman of Shunem, she persuades Elisha to eat with her and has a small upper room furnished for him.
33139: She asks nothing for herself, but Gehazi notes she has no son and her husband is old. Elisha promises a son, and she bears one the next year.
33141: The boy dies in her arms. She lays him on Elisha's bed, rides to Mount Carmel, clings to Elisha's feet and will not leave without him. Elisha prays, stretches himself on the child, and he lives.
33143: Warned of a seven-year famine, she lives among the Philistines. Returning to claim her land, she arrives just as Gehazi is telling the king her story, and the king restores everything.
33144: The woman of Shunem, a town in the Jezreel Valley, was a wealthy and generous Israelite who gave Elisha a room to stay in on his travels. She asked for nothing, but Elisha promised her a son. When the boy died, she went straight to Elisha with fierce determination, and he raised him to life. Years later the king restored her land after hearing her story. She is one of the most strong-willed and admirable figures in the Elisha stories.
33145: A 'great woman' of Shunem who provided for Elisha (2 Kgs 4:8-10). Promised and given a son (2 Kgs 4:16-17). Son raised (2 Kgs 4:32-37). Moved to Philistia during famine and had her land restored (2 Kgs 8:1-6). Hebrews may allude to her among 'women who received back their dead' (Heb 11:35).
33146: Her story, with the widow of Zarephath's, is seen as a foreshadowing of resurrection; Jesus' raising of the son of the widow of Nain at nearby Nain is often compared.
33147: Composed, self-reliant and direct; says 'it is well' through her grief and refuses to let go until help comes.
33153: He relays Elisha's messages and points out that the woman has no son.
33155: Sent ahead with Elisha's staff to lay on the dead child, he reports, 'The child has not awakened.'
33157: After Elisha refuses Naaman's gifts, Gehazi runs after him, lies that Elisha wants silver and clothes, and hides them. Elisha confronts him, and Naaman's leprosy clings to Gehazi and his descendants.
33158: Tells the king of Elisha's deeds
33159: Later he recounts Elisha's miracles to the king, just as the Shunammite arrives.
33160: Gehazi was the servant of the prophet Elisha. He was practical and observant, but when Elisha refused payment from the Aramean general Naaman, Gehazi secretly ran after him and lied to get silver and clothing. Elisha exposed him, and Naaman's skin disease came upon him. He appears once more, telling the king about Elisha's great deeds. His story contrasts a foreign general who learns grace with an Israelite insider who turns it into profit.
33161: Elisha's servant (2 Kgs 4:12). Could not wake the boy with the staff (2 Kgs 4:31). Took gifts from Naaman by deception (2 Kgs 5:20-24). Struck with leprosy 'white as snow' (2 Kgs 5:27). Later told the king Elisha's deeds (2 Kgs 8:4-5).
33162: Rabbinic lists name him among commoners who lost their share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2), and later stories cast him as a sceptic; this is tradition, not text.
33163: Often paired with Judas and with Ananias and Sapphira as a warning against greed in ministry. Some suggest 2 Kgs 8 shows him partly restored, since he speaks with the king; others take the stories as out of order (debated).
33164: Quick, practical and a little calculating; talks fast when he thinks no one is watching.
33169: Feeds Elijah with her last meal
33170: Gathering sticks to cook a final meal for herself and her son, she is asked by Elijah to make him a cake first. She trusts his promise, and her jar of flour and jug of oil do not run out through the drought.
33172: Her son dies and she blames Elijah. He carries the boy upstairs, cries to the LORD and stretches himself on him three times. The boy lives, and she says, 'Now I know that you are a man of God.'
33174: In Nazareth Jesus points out that among many widows in Israel, Elijah was sent only to this foreign widow.
33175: The widow of Zarephath lived in a Phoenician town near Sidon, Jezebel's homeland, during the great drought. Down to her last handful of flour, she fed Elijah first on the strength of God's promise, and her supplies lasted until the rain. When her son died, Elijah raised him, the first resurrection recorded in the Bible. Jesus later used her to show that God's mercy reached outsiders, which enraged his hometown.
33176: A widow at Zarephath of Sidon commanded to feed Elijah (1 Kgs 17:9). Flour and oil did not fail (1 Kgs 17:16). Her son died and was revived (1 Kgs 17:17-22). She confessed Elijah as a man of God whose word is truth (1 Kgs 17:24). Jesus cites her (Luke 4:25-26).
33178: Some midrashic traditions identify her son with the prophet Jonah (tradition).
33179: Seen as an example of Gentile faith and of God's care for the poor and foreign, and as a foreshadowing of resurrection.
33180: Honest and worn down by hardship, plain about her poverty and her grief; slowly moving from desperation to faith.
33189: At Horeb God tells Elijah to anoint Hazael king over Aram as an instrument of judgment.
33191: Sent by the sick Ben-hadad to consult Elisha, he is told he will be king and will do terrible harm to Israel. Elisha stares at him and weeps.
33192: The next day he smothers Ben-hadad with a wet cloth and becomes king.
33194: He takes all Israel's land east of the Jordan and oppresses Israel through Jehu's and Jehoahaz's reigns.
33196: He captures Gath and turns toward Jerusalem; Joash of Judah buys him off with the temple treasures.
33197: Hazael was an official of Ben-hadad who murdered his master and became king of Aram-Damascus in about 842 BC. Elisha wept when he foresaw the cruelty Hazael would inflict on Israel. As king he took all of Israel's territory east of the Jordan, pressed deep into Philistia and forced Judah to pay him off. Assyrian records call him 'son of a nobody', meaning a usurper, and he is widely thought to be the author of the Tel Dan inscription, which mentions the 'house of David'.
33198: To be anointed by Elijah (1 Kgs 19:15). Elisha foretold his kingship and cruelty (2 Kgs 8:12-13). Killed Ben-hadad (2 Kgs 8:15). Fought Joram at Ramoth-gilead (2 Kgs 8:28). Reduced Israel (2 Kgs 10:32). Took Gath; Joash paid tribute (2 Kgs 12:17-18). His son Ben-hadad lost cities to Israel (2 Kgs 13:24-25). Amos announces fire on 'the house of Hazael' (Amos 1:4).
33199: Shalmaneser III's inscriptions call Hazael a 'son of nobody' who seized the throne (scholarly-consensus). Most scholars attribute the Tel Dan Stele, which claims victory over a king of Israel and a king of the 'house of David', to Hazael, though some debate the authorship and reading (debated).
33201: The text records no anointing by Elijah; Elisha's encounter is usually read as fulfilling Elijah's commission through his successor.
33202: Smooth and deferential in front of the prophet, ruthless in private; speaks with false modesty ('what is your servant, a dog?').
33207: royal name of several kings of Aram-Damascus
33209: Ben-hadad son of Tabrimmon takes Asa's gold, breaks his treaty with Baasha and conquers towns in northern Israel.
33211: Ben-hadad, with thirty-two allied kings, demands Ahab's wealth and family. While drinking in his tent, his army is routed.
33213: Claiming Israel's god rules only the hills, he fights in the plain and loses again. Ahab spares him on generous terms, and a prophet condemns Ahab for it.
33215: His raids are foiled by Elisha's warnings; an army sent to seize Elisha at Dothan is struck blind. His siege of Samaria ends when his army flees at a noise from the LORD.
33217: Sick, he sends Hazael to ask Elisha if he will recover; Hazael smothers him and takes the throne.
33218: Ben-hadad, 'son of Hadad' (the Aramean storm god), was a name or title used by several kings of Damascus, Israel's main rival to the north in the ninth and eighth centuries BC. The Bible mentions at least two and probably three: Ben-hadad son of Tabrimmon, whom Asa hired against Baasha; the Ben-hadad who fought Ahab and Joram and was murdered by Hazael; and Hazael's son Ben-hadad, who lost cities back to Israel. Scholars debate whether the first two are the same man and how the second relates to the 'Hadadezer' of Assyrian records.
33219: Son of Tabrimmon, son of Hezion (1 Kgs 15:18). Fought Ahab at Samaria and Aphek (1 Kgs 20:1-34). Besieged Samaria in Elisha's day (2 Kgs 6:24). Killed by Hazael (2 Kgs 8:15). Ben-hadad son of Hazael defeated three times by Jehoash of Israel (2 Kgs 13:24-25). The 'strongholds of Ben-hadad' will burn (Jer 49:27; Amos 1:4).
33220: Some count Ben-hadad I (Asa's time), Ben-hadad II (Ahab's foe) and Ben-hadad III (Hazael's son); others think Ben-hadad I and II were one long-reigning king. Assyrian records name Hadadezer as Damascus' king at the battle of Qarqar in 853 BC, leading some to think 'Ben-hadad' in 1 Kgs 20 is a title or that the stories have been rearranged (debated).
33222: The Melqart Stele mentions a 'Bar-Hadad', and the Zakkur inscription names Bar-Hadad son of Hazael (scholarly-consensus on Zakkur; the Melqart reading is debated).
33223: Boastful and theatrical in strength, wheedling in defeat; fond of grand demands and drinking-tent bravado.
33231: When Athaliah kills the royal family, his wife Jehosheba rescues baby Joash, and they hide him in the temple for six years.
33233: He organises the guards and Levites, crowns the seven-year-old Joash in the temple, and has Athaliah executed outside the temple grounds.
33234: He makes a covenant between the LORD, king and people; the people tear down Baal's temple and kill its priest Mattan.
33236: Joash does right all the days Jehoiada instructs him, including repairing the temple with a collection chest.
33238: He dies at 130 and is buried with the kings because he had done good in Israel.
33239: Jehoiada was the chief priest in Jerusalem who saved David's royal line. When Queen Athaliah murdered the heirs to the throne, he and his wife Jehosheba hid the infant Joash in the temple for six years, then staged a carefully planned coup, crowned the boy and had Athaliah executed. He led a covenant renewal, cleared out Baal worship and guided Joash for decades. After his death Joash turned away and even had Jehoiada's son Zechariah stoned.
33240: Organised the coronation of Joash (2 Kgs 11:4-12). Ordered Athaliah's death (2 Kgs 11:15). Made a covenant (2 Kgs 11:17). Joash did right all his days because Jehoiada instructed him (2 Kgs 12:2). Married Jehosheba, daughter of King Jehoram (2 Chr 22:11). Died at 130, buried with kings (2 Chr 24:15-16). After his death Joash turned to idols and killed his son Zechariah (2 Chr 24:17-22). Not the father of Benaiah, who belongs to David's time.
33241: Many link Jesus' words about the blood of Zechariah 'between the sanctuary and the altar' (Luke 11:51) to Jehoiada's son, since Chronicles ends the Hebrew Bible; Matthew's 'son of Barachiah' complicates this (debated).
33242: Authoritative, patient and strategic; a priest who speaks of covenant and acts with a soldier's planning.
33248: He wins back territory from Lebo-hamath to the Dead Sea, as the prophet Jonah son of Amittai had foretold, because the LORD saw Israel's bitter suffering.
33250: Amos prophesies that God will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword. The priest Amaziah of Bethel reports this to the king and tells Amos to go home to Judah.
33251: Jeroboam II, son of Joash and great-grandson of Jehu, reigned over Israel for forty-one years (about 793 to 753 BC, including a co-regency with his father). The verdict of the text is that he did evil, keeping the sins of Jeroboam I. Yet God used him to restore Israel's borders, and his reign was the northern kingdom's last era of wealth and power. The prophets Amos and Hosea show the dark side of that prosperity: luxury for the rich, injustice for the poor and empty religion. Within thirty years of his death the kingdom had fallen to Assyria.
33252: Reigned forty-one years in Samaria and did evil (2 Kgs 14:23-24). Restored Israel's border as Jonah prophesied (2 Kgs 14:25). God saved Israel by him because he had not said he would blot out Israel's name (2 Kgs 14:26-27). Recovered Damascus and Hamath (2 Kgs 14:28). Named in the headings of Hosea and Amos (Hos 1:1; Amos 1:1). His son Zechariah reigned six months (2 Kgs 15:8-12).
33253: A seal from Megiddo inscribed 'Shema servant of Jeroboam' is usually linked to Jeroboam II, and the Samaria ostraca are often dated to his reign (scholarly-consensus on the seal's date range; attribution debated).
33254: Self-assured and prosperous; speaks like a successful king who sees no need for prophets' warnings.
33258: Kills Shallum and takes the throne
33259: Coming up from Tirzah, he kills Shallum, who had reigned only a month after assassinating Zechariah.
33261: When Tiphsah refuses to open its gates, he sacks it and rips open its pregnant women.
33263: When Pul (Tiglath-pileser III) of Assyria invades, Menahem pays a thousand talents of silver, raised by taxing every wealthy man fifty shekels, to keep his throne.
33264: Menahem seized Israel's throne in a coup and reigned about ten years (around 752 to 742 BC). The verdict of the text is that he did evil all his days. He was notoriously brutal, and he kept power by paying a huge tribute to the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III (called Pul). Assyrian annals list 'Menihimmu of Samaria' among their tribute-payers, one of several points where the Bible and Assyrian records match. His son Pekahiah was murdered by Pekah after two years.
33265: Son of Gadi; killed Shallum (2 Kgs 15:14). Sacked Tiphsah with atrocities (2 Kgs 15:16). Reigned ten years and did evil (2 Kgs 15:17-18). Paid Pul a thousand talents (2 Kgs 15:19-20). Succeeded by his son Pekahiah (2 Kgs 15:22).
33266: Tiglath-pileser III's annals record tribute from Menahem, usually dated about 740-738 BC; this creates tension with Thiele's end date of 742 and is one reason chronologies differ (debated).
33267: Brutal, transactional and wary; speaks of silver and survival.
33273: Short reign view (Albright and others, 20 years read as a later total)
33276: As an officer, with fifty men of Gilead, he kills King Pekahiah in the citadel of Samaria.
33278: With Rezin of Damascus he attacks Jerusalem to force Ahaz into an anti-Assyrian alliance. Isaiah tells Ahaz not to fear these 'two smouldering stumps of firebrands'.
33280: He kills 120,000 Judeans in a day; the prophet Oded persuades the army to free the captives.
33282: Tiglath-pileser III takes Gilead, Galilee and Naphtali and deports the people. Hoshea son of Elah assassinates Pekah.
33283: Pekah, son of Remaliah, was an army officer who killed King Pekahiah and took Israel's throne. The text gives him twenty years, which Thiele explains by a rival reign in Gilead from about 752 BC before he ruled in Samaria from about 740 to 732 BC; others think the number is a later miscalculation. The verdict of the text is that he did evil. He joined Rezin of Damascus against Assyria and attacked Judah, prompting Isaiah's famous Immanuel prophecy. Assyria responded by stripping Israel of Galilee and Gilead, and Pekah was murdered by Hoshea.
33284: Killed Pekahiah (2 Kgs 15:25). Reigned twenty years and did evil (2 Kgs 15:27-28). Lost territory to Tiglath-pileser (2 Kgs 15:29). Killed by Hoshea (2 Kgs 15:30). Attacked Jerusalem with Rezin (2 Kgs 16:5; Isa 7:1). Isaiah dismisses him as 'the son of Remaliah' (Isa 7:4-9).
33285: Thiele and many followers posit an overlapping rival reign; others (for example Albright, Galil) shorten his reign and treat the twenty years as a later editorial figure (debated).
33286: Tiglath-pileser III claims that Israel overthrew 'Paqaha' and that he installed 'Ausi' (Hoshea) as king (scholarly-consensus).
33287: Bold, hard-edged and anti-Assyrian; a soldier-politician gambling on alliances.
33294: He conspires against Pekah and kills him.
33296: Shalmaneser V comes against him and he becomes a tribute-paying vassal.
33297: Seeks Egypt's help and is imprisoned
33298: He sends envoys to 'So, king of Egypt' and stops paying tribute. Shalmaneser arrests and imprisons him.
33299: After a three-year siege Samaria falls in Hoshea's ninth year, and the Assyrians deport Israel. The northern kingdom ends.
33300: Hoshea, son of Elah, was the last king of the northern kingdom of Israel, reigning about nine years (around 732 to 723/722 BC). He killed Pekah and ruled as an Assyrian vassal, then gambled on help from Egypt and stopped paying tribute. Assyria imprisoned him, besieged Samaria for three years and deported its people. The verdict of the text is that he did evil, 'yet not as the kings of Israel who were before him'. 2 Kings 17 follows his reign with a long sermon on why Israel fell.
33301: Killed Pekah (2 Kgs 15:30). Reigned nine years; did evil, but not like his predecessors (2 Kgs 17:1-2). Became Shalmaneser's vassal, then conspired with So of Egypt and was imprisoned (2 Kgs 17:3-4). Samaria taken in his ninth year (2 Kgs 17:6). Israel fell because they sinned against the LORD (2 Kgs 17:7-23).
33302: Tiglath-pileser III claims to have placed Hoshea on the throne. 'So' is variously identified with Osorkon IV, with Tefnakht, or read as the city of Sais (debated). Both Shalmaneser V and Sargon II claimed the capture of Samaria (debated).
33303: The Talmud suggests Hoshea was judged less harshly because he removed guards that Jeroboam had set to stop pilgrims going to Jerusalem (tradition).
33304: Anxious and calculating, a vassal king playing great powers against each other with too few cards.
33309: Earlier end to match Hezekiah's accession in 2 Kgs 18:1
33312: He makes his son 'pass through the fire', following the abhorrent practices of the nations.
33314: Threatened by Rezin and Pekah, he is told by Isaiah to stand firm in faith and to ask for a sign. He piously refuses, and Isaiah gives the sign of Immanuel anyway.
33316: He sends temple and palace silver and gold to Tiglath-pileser: 'I am your servant and your son.' Assyria takes Damascus and kills Rezin.
33318: Visiting Tiglath-pileser in Damascus, he sends a model of an altar to the priest Uriah, installs it in the temple and moves the bronze altar aside.
33320: Under pressure, he sacrifices to the gods of Damascus, cuts up the temple vessels and closes the doors of the LORD's house.
33321: Ahaz, son of Jotham, reigned over Judah for sixteen years, roughly 735 to 715 BC (the exact dates are debated because of overlapping reigns). The verdict of the text is that he 'did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD' and was one of Judah's worst kings: he sacrificed his son in fire and brought foreign worship into the temple. When Israel and Aram attacked him, Isaiah urged him to trust God, but he turned to Assyria and became its vassal. Isaiah's Immanuel prophecy was first spoken to him. His son Hezekiah reversed his policies.
33322: Reigned sixteen years; did not do right, burned his son as an offering (2 Kgs 16:2-4). Attacked by Rezin and Pekah (2 Kgs 16:5). Paid Tiglath-pileser for help (2 Kgs 16:7-8). Built a copy of the Damascus altar (2 Kgs 16:10-16). Shut the temple doors (2 Chr 28:24). Isaiah's encounter and the Immanuel sign (Isa 7:1-17). The 'dial of Ahaz' (2 Kgs 20:11; Isa 38:8). In Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:9).
33324: Jewish interpreters and many modern scholars see the sign as first fulfilled in a child born in Ahaz's time (perhaps Hezekiah or Isaiah's son). Matthew applies it to Jesus' virgin birth (Matt 1:22-23); Christians variously see direct prediction, double fulfilment, or typological fulfilment (debated).
33325: A clay bulla reads 'Belonging to Ahaz son of Jotham, king of Judah', and Tiglath-pileser III lists 'Jehoahaz of Judah' among tribute-payers (scholarly-consensus).
33326: Politically clever and spiritually evasive; uses pious words ('I will not test the LORD') to avoid trusting him.
